stem: Your team uses a Declarative Automation Bundle to deploy a job that queries a warehouse. The job must use different warehouse IDs in dev, test, and prod environments without editing the databricks.yml file between deployments. Which approach correctly configures warehouse-specific settings in the bundle?

option_texts.A: Define a warehouse_id variable in the variables block with target-specific overrides in each target configuration
option_texts.B: Hard-code the warehouse IDs directly in the job resource definition and add a deployment script to swap them
option_texts.C: Create separate databricks.yml files for each environment and switch between them during CI/CD
option_texts.D: Store the warehouse ID in a Databricks secret scope and retrieve it with a spark.conf.set() call in each notebook

drill_answer_short: Bundle variables with target overrides allow the same databricks.yml to deploy to multiple environments. Targets override variable values per environment without modifying source files.
decision_hinge: The exam guide Task 5.2 explicitly states: Understand environment-specific configuration using Declarative Automation Bundle variables and overrides while promoting the same codebase across dev, test, and prod targets. Targets override variables; the file stays unchanged.

plausible_options.B: Deployment scripts could work, but they require modifying source or adding deployment-time logic rather than using the built-in bundle variables feature.
plausible_options.C: Multiple databricks.yml files could technically work, but violates the stated requirement: the same codebase must promote without being edited.
plausible_options.D: Secrets work for sensitive values, but warehouse IDs are not secrets and belong in variables. Also, spark.conf.set() in notebooks puts infrastructure config in application code.

B.description: Misplaced: swapping values via deployment script is manual and errorprone; the bundle feature exists to avoid this.

C.description: Breaks stated requirement: the exam guide requires the same codebase promote without being edited. Multiple files means choosing which to use.

D.description: Common misconception: secrets are for credentials, not for configuration that varies by environment. Also, Spark config in notebooks couples infrastructure to application logic.

B.signal: without editing the databricks.yml file between deployments
B.requires_fact: Databricks Asset Bundles support target-specific variable overrides so the same file deploys to multiple environments without modification.

C.signal: without editing the databricks.yml file between deployments
C.requires_fact: The requirement is to promote the same codebase across environments; multiple files violate this constraint.

D.signal: warehouse IDs in dev, test, and prod environments
D.requires_fact: Bundle variables and targets are the correct abstraction for infrastructure configuration that varies by environment. Secrets are for sensitive values, not configuration.

stem: You are working in a Databricks Git folder and need to make changes to a job definition before it is deployed to production. Your team uses a branching strategy where feature development happens on branches. Which action correctly creates and switches to a new branch for your changes?

option_texts.A: Click the branch dropdown in the workspace UI Git panel and select Create Branch, enter the branch name, and confirm
option_texts.B: Run databricks bundle deploy --branch feature-name from the CLI to automatically create and switch branches
option_texts.C: Edit the databricks.yml file to add a new branch field and then re-open the workspace
option_texts.D: Use the Lakeflow Jobs UI to create a job-specific branch that applies only to that job

drill_answer_short: Databricks Git folders integrate branch management into the workspace UI. The branch dropdown provides create and switch operations without using the CLI.
decision_hinge: Task 5.1 explicitly requires: Manage your code development workflow within the Databricks workspace UI, including creating and switching between branches in Databricks Git folders. The UI Git panel is the tool for this task.

plausible_options.B: The Databricks CLI is used for bundle validation and deployment, but branch creation is a Git operation handled by Git folders in the workspace UI, not the bundle deploy command.
plausible_options.C: databricks.yml defines bundle resources and environments, not Git branches. Branch control is part of Git, not the bundle configuration.
plausible_options.D: Lakeflow Jobs do not have job-specific branches; branching is a repository-level Git concept that affects all files in the folder.

B.description: Misplaced: the CLI is for bundle operations, not Git branch management. Git folders expose branching through the workspace UI.

C.description: Fabricated: databricks.yml has no branch field. Branches are managed by Git, not by bundle configuration.

D.description: Confusable sibling: Lakeflow Jobs and Git folders are separate concepts. Git branches apply to the entire repository, not individual jobs.

B.signal: Manage your code development workflow within the Databricks workspace UI, including creating and switching between branches
B.requires_fact: Branch creation is a Git operation available in the workspace UI Git folders panel, not a bundle CLI command.

C.signal: creating and switching between branches in Databricks Git folders
C.requires_fact: Branches are created and managed through Git, not through bundle configuration files like databricks.yml.

D.signal: creating and switching between branches in Databricks Git folders
D.requires_fact: Git folders manage branches at the repository level, not per-job. All files in a branch are affected, not just one job.

stem: Your CI/CD pipeline runs databricks bundle validate to check a Declarative Automation Bundle before deployment. The validation passes, but when you run databricks bundle deploy, the deployment fails because a job references a secret that does not exist in the target environment. How should you supply the missing secret value at deploy time?

option_texts.A: Define the secret name as a bundle variable, export it as BUNDLE_VAR_<variable_name> with the secret value, and redeploy
option_texts.B: Add a deployment hook that creates the secret in the target workspace immediately before running databricks bundle deploy
option_texts.C: Embed the secret value in the databricks.yml file using encryption, then decrypt it during deployment
option_texts.D: Modify the job definition to read the secret from a different scope using spark.conf.get() instead of secrets

drill_answer_short: Bundle variables supplied via BUNDLE_VAR_ environment variables are the correct mechanism for providing secrets and configuration at deploy time without committing them to the repository.
decision_hinge: The exam guide Task 5.4 and the seed note both establish: Declare a variable in the variables block and supply its value at deploy time through an environment variable prefixed BUNDLE_VAR_. This is the documented pattern for secrets.

plausible_options.B: Pre-deployment hooks could create infrastructure, but secrets belong in the bundle variables pattern. Adding deployment logic outside the bundle complicates CI/CD.
plausible_options.C: There is no built-in bundle encryption for secrets. Obfuscation is not secret management, and secrets must not be in source control.
plausible_options.D: spark.conf.get() reads from Spark config, not Databricks secret scopes. Also, putting credential handling in notebooks couples security to application code.

B.description: Common misconception: CI/CD logic outside the bundle makes credential management fragile. The bundle variables pattern is built for this.

C.description: Fabricated: there is no encryption field or encrypt command in bundles. Secrets must not be committed in any form.

D.description: Misplaced: spark.conf is for Spark configuration, not for reading Databricks secrets. The job must reference the secret scope correctly.

B.signal: supply the missing secret value at deploy time
B.requires_fact: Bundle variables with BUNDLE_VAR_ environment variables are the standard mechanism for providing secrets at deploy time without committing them.

C.signal: supply the missing secret value at deploy time
C.requires_fact: There is no encryption mechanism in bundle configuration. Secrets must never be stored in databricks.yml or any source file.

D.signal: a job references a secret that does not exist
D.requires_fact: The job must reference the secret scope correctly; spark.conf.get() reads from Spark config, not from Databricks secret scopes.

stem: Your team has a Declarative Automation Bundle that deploys a Lakeflow Declarative Pipeline and a Lakeflow Job that depends on it. You need to deploy this bundle to three targets: dev, test, and prod. The pipeline must read data from different catalogs in each environment. Which configuration in databricks.yml correctly parameterizes the source catalog for each target?

option_texts.A: Define pipeline in resources with source.catalog set to a variable reference, then define the variable with default and override it in each target's targets block
option_texts.B: Create three separate pipeline resources in databricks.yml, one for each environment, and modify the job to conditionally select the correct one
option_texts.C: Store the catalog name in a Unity Catalog metastore and retrieve it at runtime using the job definition
option_texts.D: Hardcode the catalog for dev in the pipeline, then add a manual step to edit the bundle configuration before deploying to test and prod

drill_answer_short: Bundle variables with target-specific overrides allow a single pipeline resource to read from different catalogs per environment. Variables are substituted at deploy time based on the target.
decision_hinge: Task 5.2 and 5.3 together establish: Use Declarative Automation Bundle variables and target overrides to configure environment-specific values like catalog names. A single resource definition with variable references promotes unchanged across targets.

plausible_options.B: Multiple pipeline resources would work technically, but require duplication and manual job logic to select the correct one. Bundle variables are the standard way to avoid duplication.
plausible_options.C: Reading metadata at runtime is possible, but decouples the infrastructure configuration from the bundle definition. Bundle variables make environment configuration explicit.
plausible_options.D: Manual editing defeats the purpose of infrastructure as code and bundles. The point of bundles is to parameterize, not to hand-edit.

B.description: Misplaced: creating multiple resources avoids using the bundle variables feature. The job would need conditional logic to select which pipeline to use.

C.description: Confusable sibling: Unity Catalog stores data and metadata, not infrastructure configuration. Infrastructure config belongs in the bundle, not in the metastore.

D.description: Breaks stated requirement: manual editing means the codebase is not promoted unchanged. This violates the core principle of infrastructure as code.

B.signal: deploy this bundle to three targets: dev, test, and prod
B.requires_fact: Bundle targets with variable overrides allow one resource definition to deploy to multiple environments; duplicating the resource defeats this mechanism.

C.signal: The pipeline must read data from different catalogs in each environment
C.requires_fact: Infrastructure configuration like catalog selection is not runtime metadata; it belongs in the bundle configuration with variables and targets.

D.signal: deploy this bundle to three targets: dev, test, and prod
D.requires_fact: The core requirement is to promote the same codebase unchanged across environments; manual editing violates this.

stem: Your CI/CD system needs to validate a Declarative Automation Bundle, check for syntax errors, and confirm that all resources are correctly defined before deploying. Which Databricks CLI command performs this validation without modifying any workspace state?

option_texts.A: Run databricks bundle validate to check syntax and resource definitions without deploying
option_texts.B: Run databricks bundle deploy --dry-run to preview changes and validate configuration
option_texts.C: Run databricks bundle run to execute the bundle and report any configuration errors
option_texts.D: Run databricks bundle push to validate and synchronize the bundle with the workspace

drill_answer_short: databricks bundle validate checks the bundle configuration, syntax, and resource definitions without making any changes to the workspace or executing resources.
decision_hinge: Task 5.4 requires: Understand the Databricks CLI to validate, deploy, and manage Declarative Automation Bundles. The validate command is specifically for checking configuration before deployment.

plausible_options.B: bundle deploy --dry-run previews changes but is a deployment command; validate is the lightweight option for configuration checking.
plausible_options.C: bundle run executes the bundle resources (jobs, pipelines, etc.), which modifies workspace state and is not a validation-only operation.
plausible_options.D: There is no bundle push command; the correct command is bundle deploy to apply changes to the workspace.

B.description: Misplaced: deploy --dry-run is a deployment-related command that connects to the workspace. validate is the dedicated validation command.

C.description: Breaks stated requirement: run executes the bundle, which modifies state. The requirement is to validate without modifying workspace state.

D.description: Fabricated: there is no bundle push command in the Databricks CLI. The correct command is bundle deploy.

B.signal: validate a Declarative Automation Bundle, check for syntax errors, and confirm that all resources are correctly defined before deploying
B.requires_fact: databricks bundle validate is the command for configuration validation. deploy --dry-run is a deployment-related command.

C.requires_fact: bundle run executes the resources, which changes workspace state. Only validate performs read-only checking.

D.requires_fact: There is no bundle push command. The Databricks CLI provides validate, deploy, and run for bundle management.
